difficultyReason: Five conditional answer choices, all plausibly relevant. The scope shift between 'a drug that prolongs survival' and 'a drug that cures the disease' is buried in the stimulus. The reversed-conditional trap (D) and the too-weak trap (E) closely mimic the correct answer's structure. Solvers must track two conditional chains simultaneously.
stimulus: A pharmaceutical company recently argued that its new oncology drug should be approved for widespread use because clinical trials showed that patients who received it survived longer than those who did not. But survival duration is not the same as recovery from disease. Any drug that genuinely warrants widespread approval must do more than extend the lives of patients — it must offer a realistic prospect of curing the disease it targets. Therefore, the company's argument for approval is unsound.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No drug that merely prolongs survival without offering a realistic prospect of cure warrants widespread approval.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any drug that cures a disease also prolongs the survival of patients who receive it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Widespread approval of a drug is warranted only when clinical trials are conducted under rigorously controlled conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any drug that warrants widespread approval will prolong the survival of patients who receive it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Drugs that extend survival duration are often mistakenly approved for widespread use before sufficient evidence of curative effect is gathered.

explanations.correct: The argument's conclusion is that the company's case for approval is unsound because the drug only prolongs survival rather than offering a cure. The missing conditional link is: prolonging survival alone (without a realistic prospect of cure) is insufficient for widespread approval. Choice A supplies exactly that link in universal, negative form — no such drug warrants approval — which, combined with the premise that the drug merely prolongs survival, forces the conclusion that approval is unwarranted.
explanations.A: Correct. This is the missing conditional that closes the gap: 'prolongs survival but no realistic prospect of cure → does not warrant approval.' Combined with the fact that the drug only prolongs survival, the conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.B: Reversed-conditional trap. The argument needs 'prolongs only → not approved,' not 'cures → prolongs.' This choice runs the relation in the wrong direction and says nothing about drugs that only prolong survival.
explanations.C: Partial-bridge trap. Trial rigor is never mentioned in the stimulus; this introduces an entirely new condition and leaves the survival-vs.-cure gap unclosed.
explanations.D: Reversed-conditional trap. This says approval-worthy drugs prolong survival — but the stimulus already grants that the drug prolongs survival. What is needed is whether prolonging survival alone suffices for approval, which D does not address.
explanations.E: Too-weak trap. 'Often mistakenly approved' increases plausibility but does not entail that this particular drug's approval is unwarranted; 'often' is far short of the universal force needed to make the conclusion follow necessarily.

difficultyReason: The argument involves a two-step chain in environmental law/policy with a buried scope shift between 'economically vital' and 'entitled to an exemption.' All five choices are conditional in form and parallel in length. The reversed-conditional trap (C) and the partial-bridge trap (B) are highly seductive because they share vocabulary with the correct answer.
stimulus: Under the Coastal Development Act, no construction project may proceed in a designated wetland zone unless the project has been granted a statutory exemption. Exemptions are granted only to projects that regional planners certify as economically vital to the surrounding community. The Harborview Marina expansion has not been certified as economically vital by any regional planner. Consequently, the Harborview Marina expansion cannot lawfully proceed.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Harborview Marina expansion is located within a designated wetland zone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any project certified as economically vital by regional planners will automatically be granted a statutory exemption under the Coastal Development Act.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any project that has been granted a statutory exemption under the Coastal Development Act has been certified as economically vital by regional planners.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Regional planners have the authority to certify construction projects as economically vital only when those projects are located outside designated wetland zones.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Construction projects that lack a statutory exemption are sometimes permitted to proceed in designated wetland zones if they pose no significant environmental threat.

explanations.correct: The Coastal Development Act prohibits wetland-zone construction without an exemption. Exemptions require economic-vitality certification. The marina has no such certification, so it cannot get an exemption. But the prohibition applies only to wetland-zone projects. The missing factual link is that the Harborview Marina expansion is actually in a wetland zone. Choice A supplies exactly that, completing the chain: wetland zone → needs exemption; no certification → no exemption; therefore cannot lawfully proceed.
explanations.A: Correct. Without this fact, the Act's prohibition simply does not apply to the marina. Adding it closes the logical gap and makes the conclusion follow with necessity.
explanations.B: Partial-bridge trap. This closes the gap between certification and exemption in the affirmative direction, but the argument already tells us the marina was not certified — so the positive direction is irrelevant. What is missing is the wetland-zone premise, not the certification-to-exemption link.
explanations.C: Reversed-conditional trap. The Act already states that exemptions are granted only to certified projects (exemption → certified). Choice C re-states this in the same direction rather than supplying the missing wetland-zone fact, and it adds nothing the premises do not already contain.
explanations.D: Shift-in-subject trap. Regional planners' certification authority is not what the argument needs; even if planners could only certify non-wetland projects, the marina still lacks certification regardless of zone, leaving the conclusion's legal basis unresolved without the wetland-zone premise.
explanations.E: Too-weak and contradictory trap. 'Sometimes permitted' weakens rather than closes the gap, and an exception for environmentally benign projects would actually undermine the conclusion by suggesting the marina might lawfully proceed.

difficultyReason: Stimulus involves a scope shift between 'written in a non-native language' and 'not an authentic expression of the author's cultural identity' — a distinction easily overlooked. Five conditional answer choices of near-identical length include a reversed-conditional trap (B), a principle-wrapping trap (D), and a too-weak trap (E). Solvers must recognize that the correct answer bridges cultural identity to linguistic authenticity, not the reverse.
stimulus: Several literary scholars have argued that the novels of Josef Andric are not authentic expressions of his cultural identity because they were written in a language that was not his native tongue. This view is mistaken. Andric was demonstrably fluent in his adopted language and had immersed himself in its literary tradition for decades. No author who is fully fluent in a language and deeply immersed in its literary tradition can be said to lack the capacity for authentic expression in that language.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any author who has the capacity for authentic expression in a language can produce novels that are authentic expressions of that author's cultural identity in that language.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any author whose novels are authentic expressions of cultural identity must be fully fluent in the language in which those novels are written.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An author's cultural identity is determined primarily by the language the author spoke during childhood rather than by any language acquired later in life.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The authenticity of a literary work is best judged by the breadth of the author's immersion in the relevant literary tradition rather than by the author's native-language background.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Authors who write in non-native languages are often capable of producing works that reflect aspects of the culture associated with that language.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes that Andric is fully fluent and deeply immersed, then cites a principle to conclude he has the capacity for authentic expression. But the scholars' charge was that his novels are not authentic expressions of his cultural identity — a claim about the work, not merely the capacity. The missing link is that capacity for authentic expression in a language entails that novels written in that language can be authentic expressions of cultural identity. Choice A supplies exactly this bridge in universal, positive form, making the conclusion follow necessarily.
explanations.A: Correct. The chain becomes: fluent + immersed → capacity for authentic expression (from the stimulus's stated principle) → novels are authentic expressions of cultural identity (from A). The scholars' claim is thereby refuted with logical necessity.
explanations.B: Reversed-conditional trap. The argument needs 'capacity → authentic work,' but B gives 'authentic work → fluent,' running the conditional backward. This does not connect Andric's demonstrated capacity to the authenticity of his novels.
explanations.C: Opposite/undermining trap. This choice actually supports the scholars' view by privileging native-language upbringing as the determinant of cultural identity, which would suggest Andric's adopted-language novels are not authentic — precisely the conclusion the argument seeks to refute.
explanations.D: Principle-wrapping trap. 'Best judged by' is an evaluative standard that falls short of the universal conditional force needed; even if immersion is the best criterion, it does not necessarily follow that Andric's novels are authentic expressions of his cultural identity without the direct capacity-to-authenticity link.
explanations.E: Too-weak trap. 'Often capable' and 'aspects of the culture' both fall well short of necessity: 'often' is not 'always,' and 'aspects of the culture' is not the same as 'authentic expressions of the author's cultural identity.' The conclusion cannot be forced by a probabilistic, scope-narrowed answer choice.
